title: A closed piece of a complete space

prereqs.why: This is one of the two directions of the corollary, and the one that does the work.
The definition of closed - containing every adherent point - is used exactly once, and it is the step that finishes the proof.
The argument starts from an arbitrary Cauchy sequence and has to produce a limit for it.

statement:
**Proposition.** Let $(X,d)$ be a complete metric space and let $E \subseteq X$
be closed. Then $E$, with the metric inherited from $X$, is complete.

The proof below is complete except for the reasons. Choose the
justification for each marked step.

Note what has to be produced: not merely a limit, but a limit **that is a
point of $E$**. That is the only difference between this and "$X$ is
complete", and it is where the closedness is spent.
hints: Write down what has to be shown before reading the steps: given a Cauchy sequence in $E$, produce a point of $E$ it converges to.
The first move is to stop thinking of the sequence as living in $E$ and think of it as living in $X$, where you know something.
Once $X$ has produced a limit $x$, there are two things left: get $x$ into $E$, and check that convergence in $X$ is convergence in $E$.

payload.claim: **Proposition.** A closed subset of a complete metric space is complete in the inherited metric.

steps.text: Let $(x_n)$ be a Cauchy sequence in $E$. We must find $x \in E$ with $x_n \to x$ in $E$.
$(x_n)$ is also a Cauchy sequence when regarded as a sequence in $X$.
So there is $x \in X$ with $x_n \to x$ in $X$.
Every $x_n$ lies in $E$, and every ball about $x$ contains $x_n$ for all large $n$, so every ball about $x$ meets $E$; that is, $x$ is adherent to $E$.
And $d(x_n, x) \to 0$ is the same statement whether the distances are read in $X$ or in $E$, so $x_n \to x$ in $E$.
Every Cauchy sequence in $E$ therefore converges in $E$, which is to say $E$ is complete. $\blacksquare$

choices: the metric on $E$ is the restriction of the metric on $X$, so the same $\eps$ and $N$ witness the Cauchy condition in both
the definition of an adherent point of $E$
$E$ is closed, and a closed set contains all of its adherent points
the metric on $E$ is the restriction of the one on $X$, so the same $\eps$ and $N$ witness convergence in both
a totally bounded set has a Cauchy subsequence
the limit of a convergent sequence is unique
